planting.note: Set grafted dormant trees into deep, well-drained soil in late winter to early spring; Cranz is a long-standing nut-growers' selection prized for vigorous growth and dependable annual cropping.

directions: Cranz is a named black walnut cultivar long favored by nut growers for combining vigorous, upright growth with heavy, consistent nut set once the tree reaches bearing age. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and full sun, and keep it well clear of gardens and orchards, since black walnut roots and fallen leaves release juglone that suppresses many other plants. A second seedling or grafted black walnut nearby improves pollination and fill, though established Cranz trees crop reliably on their own. Gather nuts promptly after they drop and remove hulls quickly to prevent staining and mold before curing kernels for storage.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant dormant grafted stock in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in early spring; Elmer Myers is grown chiefly for kernels that separate from the shell in large, unbroken halves.

directions: Elmer Myers is a Pennsylvania-origin black walnut selection valued above most seedling trees for its unusually easy cracking and high proportion of whole kernel halves, a trait that matters more for black walnut than almost any other quality since wild-type nuts are notoriously hard to pick clean. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil with full sun exposure and generous spacing, since mature trees form a broad, heavy canopy. Because black walnut is wind-pollinated and only partially self-fruitful, siting a second cultivar or seedling within range improves nut set. Harvest as hulls soften and darken, hull promptly, and cure kernels in a dry, ventilated spot for a few weeks before eating or storing.

planting.note: Set grafted trees while dormant into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ohio is one of the earliest black walnut selections still propagated by nut growers today.

directions: Ohio is one of the oldest named black walnut cultivars still in circulation, selected in the early twentieth century for a thinner shell and better flavor than typical wild seedling trees. It remains a benchmark cultivar in regional nut variety trials and is often planted alongside newer releases for comparison. Give it deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and wide spacing to accommodate its eventual size, and locate it away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to root-zone juglone. Plant a second distinct black walnut nearby to improve pollination, and harvest nuts as soon as hulls loosen to reduce staining and kernel darkening.

common_name: Nanking Chinese Chestnut (Historic USDA Blight-Resistant Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Nanking traces to an early USDA introduction of Chinese chestnut germplasm used to rebuild blight-resistant chestnut orchards in the eastern United States.

directions: Nanking descends from one of the original USDA Chinese chestnut introductions brought into the United States in the early twentieth century as breeders searched for blight-resistant replacements for the dying American chestnut. Surviving trees of this stock later supplied scionwood used in several of the twentieth century's most influential chestnut breeding programs in the eastern United States. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a second genetically distinct chestnut nearby, since Chinese chestnut is largely self-incompatible. It bears younger and more reliably than American chestnut, and its resistance to Cryphonectria blight makes it far more durable in the humid Southeast. Collect nuts from the ground as spiny burrs split in early fall, and refrigerate briefly to sweeten the kernels before eating.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

scientific_name: Castanea dentata x mollissima x crenata 'Clapper'

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Clapper is a USDA-released trihybrid combining American, Chinese, and Japanese chestnut parentage for blight resistance with a more American-chestnut-like growth habit.

directions: Clapper is a mid-twentieth-century USDA release combining American, Chinese, and Japanese chestnut ancestry in an effort to pair the tall, timber-like form of American chestnut with the blight resistance of its Asian relatives. It grows straighter and taller than pure Chinese chestnut orchard types, making it of interest for both nut production and reforestation plantings in blight-affected eastern woodlands. Site it in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and plant a second unrelated chestnut cultivar nearby for pollination, since chestnuts set poorly without cross-pollination. Harvest burrs as they split and yellow in early autumn, and store cured nuts cold and slightly moist to preserve sweetness.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maridonne is a French hybrid chestnut bred for resistance to Phytophthora ink disease, a serious problem in wet, poorly drained southern soils.

directions: Maridonne was bred by French chestnut researchers as a European-Japanese hybrid combining large, high-quality nuts with strong resistance to Phytophthora ink disease, a root and collar rot that thrives in the heavy, wet soils common across much of the Gulf South. It flowers in midseason and is commonly paired with other European-Japanese hybrid cultivars for cross-pollination, since chestnuts rarely set a full crop without a compatible partner nearby. Grow it in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and improve drainage on heavier clay sites to further reduce ink disease pressure. Harvest nuts from the ground as burrs split in autumn, and cure briefly before eating to allow the starches to convert to sugars.
sources: INRA (Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique)
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage color deepens with more direct sun.

directions: Purple Giant Filbert is grown as much for its deep maroon-purple spring foliage, which mellows toward green-purple by late summer, as for its edible filbert-type nuts borne in husked clusters each fall. It makes a striking specimen shrub or informal hedge and colors best with several hours of direct sun daily, though it tolerates light shade. Plant a second, genetically distinct hazel nearby for reliable nut set, since Corylus is wind-pollinated and self-incompatibility is common. Prune out old, crowded stems in late winter to renew vigor and maintain strong leaf color on fresh growth, and rake up and destroy any leaves showing eastern filbert blight cankers.
